Abandoned
This defeats most of the purpose of entity manager supporting multiple systems with a single binary.

I'd also say, we shouldn't allow selecting on a per folder basis.  That incentivizes people to put configs in their companies folder even if they don't belong (such as in the case of a shared NIC, or other add in card).

> This defeats most of the purpose of entity manager supporting multiple systems with a single binary.

- The default is still to deploy all configurations.
- This is simply an example of how this feature can be used.
- I do not expect anyone to blindly copy-paste this regex.
- A more realistic regex here would also account for the PSU jsons
  or other common jsons which need to be there for a 'complete' image.
- Users may deploy as many configs as they want with this feature,
  there is no limit to the amount of systems that can be supported.
  So i do not see the point here.

> I'd also say, we shouldn't allow selecting on a per folder basis. That incentivizes people to put configs in their companies folder even if they don't belong (such as in the case of a shared NIC, or other add in card).

The current incentive for people is to
- delete upstream configs
- deploy their own configs
- keep their configs downstream

as this keeps them in control of their configurations which they validated for their particular use-case and hardware setup.

For example this instance (and the surrounding configs which they deploy),

https://github.com/MCT-BMC/tyan_openbmc/blob/master/meta-mct/meta-s8030/recipes-phosphor/configuration/entity-manager/0005-remove-NVME-P4000.json.patch

or this 

https://github.com/ampere-openbmc/openbmc/blob/c47375f672babf39d3d399c2971a14fc527feb4c/meta-ampere/meta-jefferson/recipes-phosphor/configuration/entity-manager/mtjefferson_cbp2980.json

I would prefer people to have their configurations upstream instead.

> I'd also say, we shouldn't allow selecting on a per folder basis. That incentivizes people to put configs in their companies folder even if they don't belong (such as in the case of a shared NIC, or other add in card).

Did this actually happen in EM?

If someone puts something in a wrong place, you can still veto that or move it afterwards. There is nothing preventing you from reviewing changes just because companies might be maintaining configurations in some sub-directory.

I am reading this as "Let's not have folders since then people might put things into the wrong  folder".
I have reworked the patch to not rely on regex.

> as this keeps them in control of their configurations which they validated for their particular use-case and hardware setup.

And for their downstream, that might absolutely be the right decision for maintenance reasons.  Here in upstream, we get to look at OpenBMC as a whole of more than one platform.  Platform specifics (if we want to support that) would go in meta layers.

> I would prefer people to have their configurations upstream instead.

I'm confused, what's stopping them from upstreaming those?  The first looks like we missed a probe for manufacturer, which I'd really like to start requiring on all new configs, but we haven't gotten there yet.  For that device, I think it's already been fixed?

Fwiw, the second one also has a bad probe:
```
        "xyz.openbmc_project.FruDevice({'BOARD_PART_NUMBER': 'CBP2980'})"
```

Is the fix to this just that we need to require all FRU probes to have some level of manufacturer matching?  That seems a lot easier to maintain and support (we can get a CI check for it) than trying to segment who wants which configs.

> Did this actually happen in EM?

Yep, still exists on master too:
https://github.com/openbmc/openbmc/blob/master/meta-amd/meta-daytonax/recipes-phosphor/configuration/entity-manager/daytonax-baseboard.json

> And for their downstream, that might absolutely be the right decision for maintenance reasons. 

In my perspective, having a downstream is somewhat of a last resort

> Platform specifics (if we want to support that) would go in meta layers.

I disagree 😊,  EM ```configurations/``` directory is full of platform specific board configurations.


> Yep, still exists on master too:

Which is only reinforcing my argument. 

https://github.com/openbmc/openbmc/blob/36d626ab36102f241ce100f5cf485ef277c7e942/meta-amd/meta-daytonax/recipes-phosphor/configuration/entity-manager_%25.bbappend

Stuff like this shows how people want EM to work. They want to deploy configuration for their board only. Since their BMC firmware image is intended to support that board and not capable to support another board.


So there is no benefit for them to have extra configuration files which they will never use.
Closing this comment thread since it's been inactive for 2 months. Let me know if there are still any concerns 😊
benchmarks please

+1, and show some effort that we've tried to optimize this in other ways.  This seems counter to the entity-manager stated goal of

"Reduce the amount of code that is different between platforms"

This would make the config different.
https://github.com/openbmc/entity-manager?tab=readme-ov-file#goals

> benchmarks please

Agree, i can provide benchmarks to show there is some measurable benefit.

> +1, and show some effort that we've tried to optimize this in other ways.

Converting the .json files into .cpp files during the build step would optimize it in another way. Then EM could just use that as default and when people develop their config in ```/usr/share/entity-manager/configurations```, EM could use that to override that which is built into the binary.

This would eliminate the parsing step. However it is not optimal
since there would still be configuration which is not needed.

>  This seems counter to the entity-manager stated goal of
  "Reduce the amount of code that is different between platforms"
  This would make the config different.

There should be no observable difference besides a reduced EM startup delay,

There is some leeway in this feature for how far one wants to go with determining compatibility. 

We can start out by looking into the baseboard compatibility which is easy to determine. So that is phase 1.

Then perhaps look into power supplies. Should also be easy to determine the compatibility there.

Covering baseboards and power-supplies will already go a long way.

How does is this value get maintained as we add components?  Every time we add a pcie add in card, are we going to ask every platform maintainer with a pcie port on their system to update their regex?  That seems like a lot of effort for very little payoff.

That's why it is a list of regex and not plain strings 😊.

If one wants to support all PSU, go with ```psu-*```

If one wants to support only the CRPS PSU, go with ```psu-crps```

If one wants to support all the pcie hardware, go with ```pcie-*```

So there is a choice for the yocto layer maintainer in how fine-grained they want to configure this.

Now the time where someone may need to adjust their regex list is when we annotate a new category of hardware. In that case the config would no longer be installed automatically.

For example if we start with the baseboards, my regex would look something like ```tyan-*```. Then at a later state we may start evaluating the PSU compatibility and i may need to adjust the regex to be like ```tyan-* psu-*```.

I would assume anyone using this feature to fine-grain pick their configuration will be able to keep up with those changes.

For people who don't care and just want to have support support for everything they can always leave the meson option as default.
